title: General prevention of idiosyncratic immune-mediated drug injury

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general way to prevent serious drug injuries caused by an individual patient’s immune response. It could work through either of two routes: identifying hazardous drug candidates before widespread human exposure, or identifying susceptible patients before prescribing a causative drug. The defining advance would be reliable performance on drugs or drug–allele pairs outside those used to develop the method.

The biological starting point is that susceptibility can depend on how a drug interacts with a person’s immune system. Daly’s 2025 review describes associations with particular human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles and evidence that these alleles can present self-peptides inappropriately to T cells in the liver. It also identifies genetic contributors beyond HLA. These findings motivate prediction that combines drug properties with patient biology, but do not establish a universal recipe for predicting injury.

The intended scope is broader than a test for one known drug reaction. Abacavir screening provides a successful drug-specific precedent, while the supplied evidence on broader prediction chiefly concerns drug-induced liver injury. General prevention across drugs, and extension to immune-mediated injury in skin, bone marrow, or other organs, remain proposed capabilities rather than demonstrated achievements.

significance.text: If achieved across previously untested drugs, this capability would turn a serious source of uncertainty in prescribing and drug development into an actionable prevention decision. Developers could avoid advancing some injurious candidates, and clinicians could avoid exposing susceptible patients to particular drugs. Daly’s review documents both prevention goals; the judgment that their general realization would be revolutionary is a synthesis of those goals and the drug-specific clinical precedent.

Abacavir shows why the idea is consequential: a genetic screening strategy prevented immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity within a prospective trial. The analogy has a firm boundary, however. Success for one drug and one HLA association does not establish that equally useful markers exist for other drugs, that their predictive values will transfer, or that all clinically suspected reactions will disappear.

As a conditional downstream possibility, a sufficiently selective patient test could preserve access to a useful medicine for many patients while directing those at greatest risk toward alternatives. A development-stage test could reduce exposure to hazardous candidates. These benefits depend on sensitivity, false-positive exclusions, available alternatives, and the consequences of withholding treatment; a prediction has value only if acting on it improves outcomes.

The direct advance would concern the targeted immune-mediated injury class. It would not by itself predict therapeutic efficacy, appropriate dose, or non-immune toxicity. Prediction from chemical structure alone is one possible proposed route, but the documented involvement of HLA, T-cell responses, and additional susceptibility genes makes patient-specific information a plausible requirement. The supplied evidence does not establish structure-only prediction or support general claims about detection in animals, the usual timing of these injuries, or their contribution to late drug withdrawals.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is demonstrated generalization from biological associations to clinically useful prevention on new drugs or new drug–allele pairs. Identifying an HLA association is an important mechanistic step, but it does not by itself establish how accurately a test will identify future cases or how many patients would unnecessarily lose access to treatment. The supplied abstracts do not demonstrate a general prevention system, and they do not establish a categorical absence of every adequate screening approach.

One scientific barrier is integrating multiple contributors to susceptibility. Daly describes HLA-associated antigen presentation, T-cell involvement, non-HLA genetic contributors, and, for isoniazid-only injury, a contribution from drug metabolism. A general method would have to determine which factors matter for each drug and which relationships transfer across drugs. The evidence does not establish that every reaction requires a particular matching T-cell receptor and a second immune signal, or that risk-allele carriers usually escape injury across all drugs.

An engineering implication is that a useful assay or model must connect measurable drug and patient features to injury outcomes, rather than merely detect a biological interaction. Candidate approaches would need to distinguish informative immune responses from responses that do not lead to clinically important harm, and to handle susceptibility factors that differ across populations. These are proposed design requirements inferred from the multifactorial biology, not capabilities demonstrated by the supplied studies.

A further proposed barrier is clinical validation: defining the relevant injury, separating immune-mediated outcomes from other adverse events, and observing patients long enough to test the intended use. PREDICT-1 illustrates why endpoint definitions matter, because immunologically confirmed and clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity produced different results. The original assertion that human-specific adaptive immunity is the definitive limitation of preclinical cytotoxicity assays cannot be established from the supplied material; the adequacy of particular assay systems remains an open technical question.

current_state.text: In the 2008 PREDICT-1 randomized trial, prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening excluded allele-positive patients from abacavir treatment. During six weeks of observation, immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity occurred in 0% of the prospective-screening group versus 2.7% of the control group, with P<0.001. The reported negative predictive value was 100% and positive predictive value was 47.9%. These are results for the trial’s population, endpoint, and observation period, not universal performance guarantees.

Clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity still occurred in 3.4% of the screened group. Thus, the trial demonstrated prevention of a specific immunologically confirmed toxic reaction; it did not show elimination of every clinically suspected hypersensitivity event or prevention of immune-mediated injury across drugs. The supplied review supports these findings through the retained PubMed abstract rather than a full trial report.

Daly’s January 2025 review identifies amoxicillin-clavulanate and flucloxacillin as the two main examples of drug-induced liver injury with replicated genetic risk factors and understanding of the underlying mechanism. This qualified statement does not mean that only two genetic associations with liver injury exist. The same abstract describes other associations, non-HLA susceptibility factors, a simple polygenic score for amoxicillin-clavulanate injury, and more complex scores that may have broader application. It does not provide clinical performance sufficient to establish general preventive screening.

Only Daly’s PubMed abstract is available in the supplied evidence. That limits assessment of the review’s detailed methods, qualifications, and supporting studies; it does not establish that a full-text loading attempt failed. The research also attributes a statement about inadequate idiosyncratic liver-injury screening to Uetrecht’s 2025 review, but no retained source text is supplied for that article. That statement therefore remains unverified here, rather than disproved.

The supported picture is a dated drug-specific prevention success alongside continuing genetic and predictive work on liver injury. The supplied materials contain no documented freshness search establishing the field’s status on November 1, 2026. They therefore support assessment of the 2008 trial and the 2025 review statements at their stated dates, without resolving whether later work has changed the broader picture.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospectively evaluate a method on drugs or drug–allele pairs not used to build or tune it. A development-stage route would predict clinically important immune-mediated injury sufficiently well to support stopping hazardous candidates before large human exposure. A patient-screening route would prevent most serious cases while withholding the drug from only a minority of otherwise eligible recipients. These are proposed practical goals, not established numerical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective prevention demonstrated on unseen drugs or drug–allele pairs

completion_criteria.text: The two routes reflect the prevention goals described by Daly: avoiding licensing drugs that cause liver injury and avoiding prescribing causative drugs to susceptible patients. PREDICT-1 provides a precedent for prospective evaluation of patient screening. Reproducing an already established pairing would be useful confirmation, but would not alone satisfy the proposed claim of generalization to new pairings.
completion_criteria.label: Prevention generalizes beyond already established drug–allele pairings

completion_criteria.text: A proposed protocol should define clinically important injury, immune attribution, the target population, the comparator, follow-up duration, and what counts as preventing 'most' cases while excluding a 'minority' of patients. It should report uncertainty, predictive values, missed cases, unnecessary exclusions, and the outcomes of acting on test results. This would allow readers to assess both prevention and the treatment opportunities lost through screening.
completion_criteria.label: Defined prevention criteria with reported screening benefits and harms

completion_criteria.text: Convincing completion would also require independent replication and explicit practical boundaries: which drugs, populations, injury types, and clinical settings have been tested, and where performance is unknown. Extension beyond liver injury would require its own evidence. A finite set of successful prospective tests would establish demonstrated breadth across those cases, not literal universality over every drug or immune mechanism.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication with explicit tested scope and unknown performance

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with PHA-02, 'Prospective prediction of human efficacy, dose, and major toxicity before first-in-human exposure': PHA-03 addresses one difficult component of pharmacological safety. Its development-stage route overlaps with PHA-02’s toxicity prediction goal, but its patient-screening route could operate after a drug is already available. Success in PHA-03 would not establish efficacy or dose prediction, while general toxicity prediction would need explicit evidence that it covers these immune-mediated injuries.

Conceptual comparison with PHA-04, 'Antigen-chosen pharmacological control of immune memory': both concern selective immune recognition. PHA-03 could be achieved through prediction and avoidance without changing immune memory. Deliberately controlling antigen-specific memory would be a distinct intervention and is not required by the prevention concept.

Conceptual comparison with PHA-13, 'A medicine that holds its own therapeutic window without an external controller': both seek safer treatment, but their mechanisms and demonstrations differ. PHA-03 focuses on susceptibility assessment or hazardous-candidate selection. A medicine that regulates its own therapeutic window would not automatically prevent immune recognition or delayed immune injury, and a screening test would not make a medicine self-regulating.

Conceptual comparison with PHA-10, 'Severe analgesia whose efficacy is uncoupled from respiratory depression and reinforcement': both separate therapeutic benefit from harmful consequences, but PHA-10 targets particular effects of analgesic pharmacology. PHA-03 targets immune-mediated susceptibility across drugs. Evidence for either safety advance would not establish the other.

change_log.change: Preserved PHA-03’s identity and broad prevention goal while distinguishing the liver-injury evidence from proposed extensions to other organs.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence chiefly concerns liver injury and abacavir hypersensitivity; it does not demonstrate prevention across organs.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about absent screening and universal immune requirements with a bounded account of HLA, T-cell, and additional susceptibility factors.
change_log.reason: The retained abstracts support multifactorial susceptibility but do not establish universal T-cell receptor or second-signal requirements, general penetrance claims, or the definitive limitation of cytotoxicity assays.

change_log.change: Qualified the description of abacavir as a solved special case with the six-week observation period, endpoint definition, control incidence, and residual clinically diagnosed reactions.
change_log.reason: The supported success concerns immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity, not elimination of all suspected reactions or general prevention across drugs.

change_log.change: Preserved the predictive values and added their population, endpoint, and observation-period boundaries.
change_log.reason: Trial predictive values should not be presented as universal guarantees.

change_log.change: Clarified the two-main-examples statement and integrated developing polygenic scores and non-HLA contributors.
change_log.reason: Daly’s statement concerns replicated genetic findings with mechanistic understanding, not the total number of associations.

change_log.change: Separated the unverified Uetrecht screening assertion from supported findings and corrected the Daly access description.
change_log.reason: No Uetrecht text was retained, and an abstract-only record does not demonstrate a failed full-text loading attempt.

change_log.change: Retained the conditional significance while removing unsupported generalizations about animal testing, typical detection timing, and late withdrawals.
change_log.reason: Those factual assertions lack support in the supplied reviewed material and are unnecessary to explain the proposed advance.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria into prospective generalization, clinical usefulness, independent replication, and explicit practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These make the proposed capability assessable without treating suggested thresholds as established standards or finite testing as proof of universality.

change_log.change: Added distinctions from the relevant roster concepts and bounded the currency of the evidence.
change_log.reason: Related safety and immune-control goals remain separate innovations, and no supplied freshness search establishes the field’s November 2026 status.

unresolved_issues: Whether later work has demonstrated substantially broader prediction or prevention remains unknown from the supplied evidence; no documented freshness search was provided.
Uetrecht’s attributed statement about inadequate screening cannot be verified without retained source text. Its absence is not evidence that the statement is false.
Daly’s full review and the full PREDICT-1 report were not available within the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond their retained abstracts.
The clinical performance, validation populations, and practical preventive value of the described polygenic risk scores remain unspecified.
The necessity and contribution of particular T-cell receptors, additional immune signals, and assay components across different drugs remain unresolved.
Generalization to skin, bone-marrow, and other immune-mediated drug injuries requires evidence beyond the supplied liver-injury and abacavir material.
A future validation protocol must specify injury definitions, follow-up, acceptable missed-case and exclusion rates, and clinically meaningful performance for each intended use.

brief.title: Preventing harmful immune reactions to medicines
possible: Before taking a medicine, you could learn whether your immune system is likely to react in a way that causes serious injury. Doctors could choose an alternative, while drug developers could identify hazardous candidates before exposing many people.
The capability would work across medicines, including drugs or combinations of drugs and genetic variants that were not used to develop the test.
why: Patients could avoid serious harm while retaining access to medicines they can safely use. Doctors would gain a reason to choose or avoid a particular drug, and developers could stop some hazardous candidates earlier.

sources.who: Simon Mallal and the PREDICT-1 Study Team
sources.showed: A randomized trial found that genetic screening before prescribing abacavir prevented immune-confirmed hypersensitivity, a harmful immune reaction. Some patients still had clinically suspected reactions.
sources.quote: Our results show that a pharmacogenetic test can be used to prevent a specific toxic effect of a drug.
sources.cited_for: Genetic screening can prevent a specific harmful immune reaction before a patient takes the drug.
sources.not_established: Success with abacavir does not establish prevention across other medicines or elimination of every suspected reaction.

sources.showed: This review discusses prediction of drug-caused liver injury during drug development.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the problem of screening drug candidates for liver injury.
sources.not_established: A review of prediction does not itself demonstrate a general method that prevents immune-mediated drug injury.

sources.showed: Daly reviewed genetic links to drug-caused liver injury and scores combining several genetic risks. These involve HLA, immune-system genes, as well as other genes affecting immune responses and drug processing.
sources.quote: Non-HLA genes also contribute to genetic susceptibility, both as co-factors in T-cell responses and, in the case of isoniazid-only, drug metabolism.
sources.cited_for: Susceptibility involves several biological factors, including genes affecting T cells, a type of immune cell.
sources.not_established: Genetic associations and risk scores do not yet establish clinically useful prevention across previously untested drugs.

shown: Mallal and colleagues demonstrated prevention for abacavir: screening out patients with a particular genetic variant eliminated immune-confirmed reactions during the trial. Daly describes replicated genetic findings and understood mechanisms for liver injury from amoxicillin-clavulanate and flucloxacillin.
missing: A method must reliably prevent serious immune injury from drugs or drug–genetic variant combinations it was not developed on.
Tests must distinguish biological responses that cause serious harm from responses that do not.
Clinical trials must establish whether acting on predictions prevents harm without unnecessarily denying useful treatment.
Prevention of immune injury in skin, bone marrow and other organs needs its own demonstration.

milestones.label: Prospective prevention on previously untested drugs or genetic combinations
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to test predictions on drugs or drug–genetic variant combinations excluded from development. It would establish whether the method can stop hazardous candidates or protect susceptible patients.

milestones.label: Prevention extends beyond established drug and genetic risk pairings
milestones.explanation: Prevention would have to succeed beyond already established drug–genetic variant associations. Repeating a known success alone would not establish the broader capability.

milestones.label: Defined success criteria reveal screening benefits and harms
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to define injury, immune involvement, population, comparison and follow-up, then report missed cases and unnecessary exclusions. This would reveal whether prevention outweighs lost treatment opportunities.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes where prevention works
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce prevention and state which drugs, populations and injury types were tested. This would establish demonstrated breadth and leave untested uses explicit.

uncertain: Which combinations of immune responses, genetic factors and drug processing will predict injury across different medicines?
How many missed cases and unnecessary treatment exclusions would be acceptable for each intended use?
How well will genetic risk scores work across populations and translate into better patient outcomes?

page.title: Cross-drug prevention of immune-mediated drug injury
page.definition: A common method identifies hazardous medicines or susceptible patients before exposure and prevents serious injury caused by an individual's immune response. Its preventive benefit extends to drugs or drug–genetic-variant pairs excluded from the method's development.

goal.need: Prevention must reduce injury without unnecessarily excluding treatment. In PREDICT-1, the positive predictive value of HLA-B*57:01 screening for immune-confirmed abacavir hypersensitivity was 47.9%; a positive result did not make injury certain. The trial established prevention for one drug, while clinically suspected and immune-confirmed reactions gave different results.

figures.caption: Abacavir hypersensitivity during six weeks of exposure in PREDICT-1
figures.note: The trial randomized 1,956 patients from 19 countries; percentages concern patients receiving abacavir. Screening excluded HLA-B*57:01 carriers. HLA proteins display peptide fragments to immune cells. Both comparisons had P<0.001. Results were published on 7 February 2008.

statements.body: US Department of Health and Human Services Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents
statements.quote: The Panel recommends screening for HLA-B*5701 before starting patients on an abacavir (ABC)-containing regimen to reduce the risk of hypersensitivity reaction (HSR) (AI).
statements.context: The recommendation was reviewed on 10 January 2011. AI denotes a strong recommendation supported by randomized controlled trials.

statements.body: European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
statements.quote: It is therefore important to set up multicentre translational studies to advance the validation process towards reaching a clinical utility phase.
statements.context: The task-force report concerns biomarkers of immune-mediated drug reactions.

completion.title: A fixed method prevents serious immune injury on excluded drugs, with independent replication.
completion.criterion: A prediction-and-action strategy, fixed before evaluation, reduces prospectively adjudicated serious immune-mediated injury versus usual practice for drugs or drug–genetic-variant pairs excluded from its development. Independent investigators replicate preventive benefit on additional excluded drugs or pairs. Each controlled study meets its registered superiority criterion and prespecified benefit–harm criteria, including missed injuries, withheld effective treatment and harm from alternatives. Follow-up, immune attribution and seriousness are protocol-defined. Acceptance limits belong to each registered intended use.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no outside body's published test for prevention on drugs excluded from method development was found.
completion.basis: FDA and EMA biomarker-qualification guidance, CIOMS's DILI consensus, EAACI task-force reports and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for a general cross-drug prevention test and numerical benefit–harm limits; none was found. Qualification concerns a specified context of use. EAACI distinguishes clinical validity from clinical utility. The Atlas test adds transfer and independent replication to distinguish this capability from established drug-specific screening.

milestones.title: A susceptibility assay measures its biomarker accurately and reproducibly.
milestones.criterion: Establish analytical validity for the intended use: correct biomarker measurement, accuracy, precision and reproducibility. The cited framework specifies no universal numerical acceptance limits. In 2007, seven laboratories correctly typed a 10-sample HLA-B*57:01 panel; four tested a 96-sample panel containing 36 positives, with one false negative. This allele is relevant to abacavir systemic hypersensitivity and flucloxacillin liver injury. The survey did not validate cutaneous-risk alleles or clinical injury prediction.
milestones.set_by: CIOMS Working Group on Drug-Induced Liver Injury, 2020 consensus report, section 4.2.1; EAACI's 2025 report recognizes the same analytical-validity stage. CIOMS's discussion concerns liver biomarkers.
milestones.threshold_quote: the test will provide accurate and reproducible results.

milestones.title: A susceptibility test predicts immune-mediated injury in prospectively followed patients.
milestones.criterion: Establish clinical validity against injury outcomes in exposed patients, with sensitivity, specificity and predictive values appropriate to the intended use. EAACI places clinical validity in prospective studies; the cited frameworks supply no universal numerical cutoff. PREDICT-1 provides prospective evidence for systemic abacavir hypersensitivity. For liver injury, Daly reports validation of an amoxicillin-clavulanate genetic score in 133 new cases; this case–control result does not establish prospective prevention. The Taiwanese carbamazepine study supplies prospective cutaneous-injury evidence.
milestones.set_by: CIOMS, 2020 consensus report, section 4.2.1, defines clinical validation for liver biomarkers; EAACI's 2025 task-force report, section 2, Figure 1 and Table 1 note, applies the stage to drug-reaction biomarkers.
milestones.threshold_quote: the correlation of a biomarker test result with a biological process or a clinical outcome.

milestones.title: Susceptibility-guided prescribing prevents immune injury with a favourable balance of benefits and harms.
milestones.criterion: Establish preventive clinical utility in a multicentre study, assessing benefits against harms from acting on the test. Systemic hypersensitivity: PREDICT-1 demonstrated its abacavir prevention endpoints. Severe cutaneous reactions: a study published on 24 March 2011 recruited 4,877 people at 23 Taiwanese hospitals; after HLA-B*15:02 screening, no carbamazepine-associated Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis occurred over two months, versus approximately 10 expected from historical incidence of 0.23% (P<0.001). This was not a randomized comparison. No trial targeting liver-injury prevention was located.
milestones.set_by: EAACI, 2025 task-force report, section 2 and Figure 1: clinical utility evaluates benefits and harms, with multicentre studies. The cited prevention results concern individual drugs and populations.

milestones.title: A fixed method prevents serious immune injury on one drug excluded from its development.
milestones.criterion: Apply the validated method, without tuning to evaluation outcomes, to a drug or drug–genetic-variant pair excluded from development. A prospective controlled study meets its registered injury-reduction and benefit–harm criteria. This establishes transfer of preventive clinical utility before independent replication on additional excluded drugs or pairs. No qualifying result was located for any of the three injury classes. Koido's 2020 cross-drug liver-injury work evaluated susceptibility prediction, including 43 fasiglifam injury cases described by Daly; it did not evaluate preventive prescribing decisions.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; searches of regulatory guidance, CIOMS and EAACI reports, and trial registries did not identify a published protocol defining this transfer test.

not_found: No published general cross-drug prevention threshold or registered protocol testing preventive transfer to drugs excluded from method development was found.
The cited analytical- and clinical-validity frameworks do not specify numerical acceptance limits applicable to every drug-reaction predictor.
No prospective prevention trial acting on a drug-induced liver injury susceptibility score was located.
An interlaboratory analytical-validation result for cutaneous-risk alleles was not retrieved.
Publisher full texts of Uetrecht's 2025 review and the two cited NEJM trials returned HTTP 403; the trial abstracts were accessible.

results.finding: In 1,956 patients, HLA-B*5701 screening had a 100% negative predictive value for immunologically confirmed abacavir hypersensitivity.
results.detail: Patients who started abacavir were followed for six weeks; the reported positive predictive value was 47.9%.
results.quote: Screening eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reaction (0% in the prospective-screening group vs. 2.7% in the control group, P<0.001), with a negative predictive value of 100% and a positive predictive value of 47.9%.

results.finding: In 1,956 patients, screening reduced immunologically confirmed abacavir hypersensitivity from 2.7% to 0%.
results.detail: The multicentre randomized study excluded HLA-B*5701-positive patients from abacavir in the screening group.
results.quote: Screening eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reaction (0% in the prospective-screening group vs. 2.7% in the control group, P<0.001), with a negative predictive value of 100% and a positive predictive value of 47.9%.

results.finding: HLA-B*57:01 proficiency testing, 2017–2022: sample size not stated; 0.34% of reports were errors.
results.detail: The multi-laboratory scheme supports analytical accuracy for an allele relevant to drug-induced liver injury. It was designed for abacavir hypersensitivity and does not establish assay precision or validate its intended use for liver injury.
results.quote: In the last 6 years, 2017–2022, there was a 40% increase in participants and 13 errors (0.34%) with 9 false negative results, at least one of which stemmed from a pre-analytical error.

results.finding: In 1,194 lapatinib-treated patients, HLA allele carriers had a 7.7% risk of grade 3 ALT elevation.
results.detail: The prospective study supports prediction of liver injury risk, but the supplied text does not report sensitivity or specificity, or establish that predictive performance is appropriate for an intended clinical use.
results.quote: In lapatinib-treated patients, the overall risk for National Cancer Institute-Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 3 ALT elevation (> 5× upper limit of normal) was 2.1%; HLA allele carriers had an increased risk of 7.7%; in noncarriers, risk was reduced to 0.5%, comparable to ALT elevation for all patients receiving placebo.

results.finding: Among 2,173 screened allopurinol recipients, no severe cutaneous adverse reactions occurred.
results.detail: The 15-centre study used a historical comparison: seven cases were expected. It also monitored adverse events among patients given alternative treatments; three developed mild, transient rash. The study was non-randomized and limited to Han Chinese participants.
results.quote: Based on the estimated historical incidence of 0.30% per year, we expected seven cases of drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis among the 2173 participants in our study who took allopurinol.

results.finding: Among 542 screened patients with chronic renal insufficiency, 0 developed allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions.
results.detail: The prospective study involved 10 hospitals and used a historical control. It reports mild adverse reactions but does not establish the balance of benefits and harms from acting on the test. It is not the specified Taiwanese carbamazepine study.
results.quote: Nineteen patients in the prospective cohort developed mild and transient adverse reactions but none showed allopurinol-induced SCARs.

results.finding: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping agreed with a comparator in all 900 samples.
results.detail: The comparison supports measurement accuracy, but the paper does not establish assay precision or reproducibility.
results.quote: To confirm the genotyping results, the first 900 samples were also examined in parallel with a reverse line blot using an HLA sequence oligonucleotide (Dynal Biotech); the results were consistent in each sample.

results.finding: Among 2,173 HLA-B*58:01-negative patients taking allopurinol, zero developed SCARs.
results.detail: Carriers were advised to avoid allopurinol, so the prospective cohort could not establish sensitivity, specificity and predictive values against injury outcomes in both exposed genotype groups.
results.quote: Based on the estimated historical incidence of 0.30% per year, we expected seven cases of drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis among the 2173 participants in our study who took allopurinol.

results.finding: Screening was followed by zero SCARs among 2,173 allopurinol recipients, versus seven expected historically.
results.detail: The allopurinol–HLA-B*58:01 association was already known, so the study does not show transfer to an excluded drug or pair. It used a historical control and does not report registered benefit–harm criteria.
results.quote: In the present study, prospective screening by HLA-B*58:01 genotyping before allopurinol treatment in 2926 people with an indication for allopurinol treatment could successfully reduce the incidence of allopurinol induced SCARs (from seven expected cases of SCARs to none in the 2173 patients who took allopurinol).

results.finding: Among 503 HLA-B*58:01-negative patients treated with allopurinol, none developed allopurinol-induced SCARs.
results.detail: Allele-positive patients received an alternative drug, so the prospective cohort cannot establish sensitivity, specificity, or positive predictive value for allopurinol-induced injury.
results.quote: Nineteen patients in the prospective cohort developed mild and transient adverse reactions but none showed allopurinol-induced SCARs.

results.finding: HLA-B*57:01 assay: 150 buccal swabs showed 100% concordance with direct sequencing.
results.detail: The blinded panel included 68 positive samples. The authors describe the assay as reproducible, but report no quantitative precision or reproducibility results, so the full analytical-validity criterion is not established.
results.quote:
The concordance obtained by the comparison of the
results derived from the two different methods (traditional
sequencing vs dilution-direct PCR) was 100%.

results.finding: HLA-B*58:01 testing: 33 of 34 laboratories correctly typed all five samples in the first 2024 round.
results.detail: Four external quality assessment rounds assessed accuracy across laboratories and platforms using panels derived from two cell lines. Errors included false negatives and false positives. The survey provides evidence of reproducibility but does not establish assay-specific precision for the intended clinical use.
results.quote: A total of 14/17 (82.4%), 16/16 (100%), 33/34 (97.1%), and 33/33 (100%) laboratories achieved “optimal” scores.
